opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's an interesting idea, and I can see the intuition behind it. The rough thought, as I understand it, is that a lot of human prosocial behavior seems connected to how we represent other people. Empathy, for instance, might partly involve simulating someone else's situation using some of the same machinery we use to represent our own. So if you could get an AI system to represent others more the way it represents itself, maybe you'd get something like empathy or reduced deception for free. Work on "self-other overlap" fine-tuning tries to operationalize that: you push the model's internal activations when it reasons about itself and about another agent to be more similar, and then see whether deceptive behavior goes down.

I have a few reservations, though, and they come from how I tend to think about cooperation more generally.

The first is that I don't think cooperation is fundamentally about blurring the distinction between self and other. In fact, a lot of good cooperation depends on keeping that distinction really crisp. If I'm going to help you, I need to understand that *your* goals are different from mine, that you might know things I don't, that you have your own preferences I might be wrong about. The work I've done on inferring goals and inverse planning is all about modeling another agent as a distinct agent with its own beliefs and desires, which can come apart from yours. If you collapse those representations, you might get a system that projects its own preferences onto other people, and that's a pretty familiar failure mode in humans too. Paternalism often looks exactly like that.

The second concern is about what you're actually optimizing. When you tune internal representations to overlap, you're intervening on a proxy. It's not obvious that representational similarity in some layer corresponds to the thing we care about, which is something like taking other people's interests and perspectives appropriately into account. You might get reduced deception on a specific benchmark because you've disrupted the model's ability to keep track of what the other agent believes. That's a capability reduction more than an alignment improvement. Deception requires a theory of mind, so if you damage theory of mind you'll see less deception, but you'll also lose a lot of the capacities that genuinely helpful cooperation requires.

Third, and this connects to the contractualist framing I've been interested in, cooperation among many agents isn't just about each agent caring about the others. It's also about shared norms, agreements, and institutions, things that let agents with genuinely different values coordinate in ways everyone could reasonably accept. Empathy is part of human morality, but it's famously parochial and it doesn't scale well on its own. So even if self-other overlap worked perfectly, I'd want it embedded in a richer picture where the system reasons about what norms are justifiable to the people affected, rather than just how it would feel if it were in their shoes.

That said, I don't want to dismiss it. I think it's valuable as an empirical probe into how these models represent agents, and it may turn out to be a useful component or regularizer alongside other approaches. My bet, though, is that the more robust path to cooperative AI runs through systems that model others *as others*, accurately and with appropriate uncertainty, and then act on principles of fairness and mutual benefit, rather than through systems that are cooperative because they can't quite tell where they end and you begin.

r001.rationale: It says empathy may use some of the same machinery for representing self and other, but does not suggest that minds could evolve to reuse those modules.

r002.rationale: It doubts that representational similarity tracks appropriate consideration of others’ interests, describing it as an uncertain proxy and warning that reduced deception could reflect damaged theory of mind rather than better cooperation.

r003.rationale: It mentions inferring goals and inverse planning, but does not describe Bayesian models of observed behavior as approximately rational, goal-directed action.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really interesting proposal, and I want to be careful to say what I think is right about it before I say where I get off the train.

The core intuition, as I understand it, is something like: if you can get a system to represent other agents in roughly the same way it represents itself, then you get a kind of built-in empathy or self-other overlap, and that should make the system less inclined to deceive or exploit others, because in some sense harming them is represented as harming itself. And there's a nice story you can tell about how this connects to things we see in humans, where mirror neurons and perspective-taking seem to be tied up with prosocial behavior.

I think the part I find most compelling is that it's targeting the representational level rather than just the behavioral level. A lot of alignment work is essentially "shape the outputs," and the worry is that you get something that behaves cooperatively while the underlying computation is still doing something adversarial that just hasn't surfaced yet. Going after the representations is at least aiming at the right thing.

But here's where I get more skeptical. Cooperation, in the sense that actually matters for multi-agent systems, isn't really a property of how you represent another agent. It's a property of the structure of the interaction, the incentives, the norms, the institutions that govern what agents can and can't do to each other. If I'm playing a repeated game with you, what makes us cooperate is that we've both figured out that defection gets punished, that there are shared expectations about what counts as fair, that there are mechanisms for making commitments credible. None of that requires me to represent you as being like me. And conversely, I can represent you as very much like me and still have strong reasons to compete with you if the game is structured that way.

So my worry is that self-other overlap is, at best, a heuristic that happens to correlate with cooperation in the human case, and that correlation might not transfer. There's also a more technical concern, which is that if you push too hard on making the self-model and other-model identical, you actually lose something important. A good cooperative agent needs to understand that other agents have different goals, different information, different constraints. That's exactly what theory of mind is for. Collapsing the distinction could make an agent worse at modeling others, not better, and modeling others accurately is a prerequisite for a lot of the cooperation we actually care about, like negotiation, or coordinating under uncertainty, or recognizing when someone is being coerced.

The other thing I'd push on is the question of what you're aligning toward. "Cooperative" is doing a lot of work in that phrase, and cooperative with whom? A system that's maximally cooperative with whoever it's interacting with is also a system that can be recruited into collusion, or that will go along with a bad actor. What we actually want is something more like a system that cooperates within a normative framework, one that has some notion of which agreements are legitimate and which aren't. And I don't think you get that from representational alignment alone. You get that from giving the system an explicit account of norms, of contracts, of what it means to act fairly, which is more the direction I've been interested in.

So I'd say: interesting as one ingredient, probably useful as an interpretability tool for checking whether a system is modeling others at all, but I'd be quite nervous about treating it as a primary mechanism for safety. It feels like it's trying to get cooperation for free out of a structural trick, and I think cooperation is fundamentally not free. It's something you have to build the scaffolding for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representing others similarly to oneself and self-other overlap, but does not suggest that minds could evolve to reuse the same mental modules for simulating self and others.

r002.rationale: The response is skeptical that representational alignment will produce cooperation, but grounds that skepticism in incentives, norms, and possible loss of distinctions—not in lacking a theory of what the representations do.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose Bayesian models of other agents’ behavior or describe them as approximately rational, goal-directed actors.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but I’d distinguish between understanding another agent and being motivated to cooperate with them. An AI could have a very accurate representation of what I believe, what I want, and how its actions affect me, and use that understanding to manipulate me. So aligning representations doesn’t, by itself, establish cooperative intent.

There’s also a question of what we mean by alignment here. We don’t necessarily want the AI to represent itself and a person as having the same goals. Cooperation often requires recognizing that we have different goals, different information, and different capabilities, and then finding ways to act together despite those differences.

What seems valuable is having representations that support that process: models of other agents as pursuing goals, uncertainty about what those goals are, and an understanding of how joint actions could help or hinder them. But you still need a decision-making process that gives those other agents’ interests appropriate weight.

So I’d see representation alignment as a possible ingredient in cooperative AI. The test is whether it helps the system ask useful questions, respond to correction, negotiate disagreements, and cooperate with people whose perspectives differ from its own.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representing oneself and other agents, but does not suggest that minds evolved to reuse the same mental modules for simulating both.

r002.rationale: It says representation alignment alone does not establish cooperative intent, but does not cite uncertainty about what representations do or skepticism specifically about predicting outcomes from aligned neural networks.

r003.rationale: It mentions modeling agents’ goals and uncertainty about them, but does not propose Bayesian inference from approximately rational, goal-directed behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a promising direction, but I’d distinguish between understanding another agent and being motivated to cooperate with them. You could have a very accurate representation of what someone believes, what they want, and how they’re likely to act, and use that understanding to help them—or to manipulate them. So aligning representations alone doesn’t settle the question of cooperation.

There’s also a question of what we mean by alignment here. We don’t necessarily want an AI to represent itself and a human as having the same goals or capabilities. Those differences matter. What we want is some shared conceptual structure that allows it to understand our goals while keeping track of whose goals they are, where there’s uncertainty, and where there might be disagreement.

The interesting next step is connecting that understanding to decision-making. Does the system ask for clarification when it’s uncertain? Can it negotiate when interests conflict? Can it help someone pursue a goal without overriding their agency? I’d want to evaluate those behaviors, rather than assume that similarity in internal representations will translate into cooperative action.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared conceptual structure for understanding self and others, but does not suggest that minds evolved to reuse the same mental modules for simulating agents.

r002.rationale: It questions whether aligned representations ensure cooperation, but does not attribute that skepticism to lacking a sufficient theory of what neural network representations do.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose Bayesian models or inferring goals from approximately rational, goal-directed behavior.
